title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Inheritance

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be taking one of Dickens's richest, strangest, most inexhaustible novels completely apart — and putting it back together again.
Our Mutual Friend: a novel about dust heaps and inheritance, drowning and resurrection, money and the peculiar rot it spreads through everything it touches.
To help us do that, I've assembled three guests whose approaches to this novel couldn't be more productively different.
First, Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, lifelong Tory, and one of the most formidable close readers of nineteenth-century fiction alive.

Edmund believes that great novelists are first and last moral imaginations at work — and that no amount of social-historical scaffolding should obscure the simple, difficult question of how individuals behave under pressure.
Second, Professor James Blackstone — legal and social historian, and the man you want beside you when a novel takes you inside a courtroom, a workhouse, or a river dredger's boat.
James will keep us honest about what this world actually was — not just as Dickens imagined it, but as it truly was for the people living inside it.
And third, Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than I suspect even he can count.
Oliver hears what the rest of us sometimes miss — the comic timing, the theatrical rhythm, the lines that were written not for the eye but for the voice.
Gentlemen, welcome — and let's begin where the novel begins: in the dark, on the water, with a dead man who isn't quite dead.
Thank you — delightful to be here.
I want to say at the outset that Our Mutual Friend is, in my considered view, Dickens's most morally serious novel — which is saying something remarkable, given the competition.
It is a novel obsessed with the question of whether a human being can remake himself — genuinely remake himself, from the ground up.
John Harmon's situation is, on the surface, a contrivance of plot.
But Dickens uses that contrivance to pose a genuinely searching question: who are you, stripped of your name, your money, your history?
And the drowning scene answers that question with extraordinary psychological force.
I'd agree with Edmund on the psychological force — and I'd add that the manner in which Dickens renders that moment is technically astonishing.
We're inside a consciousness that has nearly ceased to exist, watching it reconstitute itself through sheer act of will.
The passage describes what happens after, as the narrator puts it,
'a downward slide through something like a tube, and then a great noise and a sparkling and crackling as of fires.'
That is the phenomenology of near-drowning rendered from the inside — and it is clinically precise.
But then comes the line that lifts it entirely out of the physical and into something stranger:
'This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!'
He addresses himself in the third person — as if consciousness, in extremis, splits from the self it is trying to preserve.
That third-person address is the thing, isn't it — it's the thing that makes you put the book down for a moment.
Because as a performer, I can tell you: the instinct to read it like inner monologue is absolutely wrong.
It has to be spoken aloud — almost barked — as if one part of the man is ordering another part to keep living.
And the rhythm — three repetitions of the name, each one more urgent than the last — that is pure theatre.
Dickens wrote for serialisation, yes — but he also wrote, I'm convinced, for the voice.
He gave public readings of his work his entire career, and you can hear it in every sentence like this one — the timing is built in.
Oliver is right about the rhythm — and I'd frame it in slightly different terms, if I may.
What Dickens is doing in that moment is essentially Johnsonian — the assertion of the will against dissolution.
Johnson believed that the great enemy of the moral life was a certain slackness — the failure to summon one's energies at the decisive moment.
Here, that summoning is literal — it is survival itself.
And it sets the template for everything John Harmon must do for the rest of the novel: choose, repeatedly, to be himself rather than the self the money and the world's expectations would make of him.
And yet — and this is where the social context matters enormously — the money he's fleeing is also the money he eventually accepts.
The dust heaps — the great mounds of London refuse from which old Harmon's fortune was built — are not merely a colourful backdrop.
By the 1860s, the trade in metropolitan dust — ash, bone, cinders, street sweepings — was a genuinely substantial industry.
There were men who made fortunes from it — and fortunes made from refuse carry a particular kind of moral taint, then as now.
The novel insists that money, regardless of its origin, deforms every relationship it enters — and I think that insistence is grounded in what Dickens actually saw around him.
The dust heaps, the river, the taxidermy — and speaking of taxidermy, there's a passage with Wegg and the stuffed specimens that I find almost unbearably funny.
The ghastly French gentleman is grinning under the firelight, and Dickens writes that this grin seems to be computing how many thousand slanderers and traitors array themselves against the fortunate.
And then — and I always want to applaud at this — comes the alligator.
The narrator tells us that the alligator's yard or two of smile
'might have been invested with the meaning, All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.'
The alligator, with its millennia of evolutionary patience, has seen this precise brand of human ingratitude before.
It is Dickens at his most cosmically amused — and it is also, underneath the joke, quietly devastating.
That passage is one of the great satirical set-pieces in the novel — and what I admire about it is the restraint.
Dickens doesn't name Wegg's vice directly — he lets the taxidermic audience pass judgment instead.
It is, in its structure, a kind of moral fable told entirely through implication.
Which is, I think, what makes Dickens finally more interesting than the reformers who shared his sympathies — he trusts the story.
And yet before we leave this opening, I want to register one more passage — because it shows the novel's capacity for something altogether darker than satire.
Bradley Headstone creeping up the staircase toward Eugene Wrayburn's chambers — it is one of the most purely threatening passages in the book.
Dickens describes 'the haggard head' — not the man, but the head — floating up the dark staircase.
And then the narrator delivers a line of almost horrible intimacy:

'If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night.'
The reader knows what Lightwood does not — and that is, of course, the source of the terror.
This is a novel equally at home in Gothic menace, Hogarthian comedy, and the most searching psychological drama — and that range is what we'll be exploring throughout.
And that range is precisely what makes this novel so rewarding — and so demanding — to unpack.
Dust and inheritance, drowning and resurrection, obsession stalking up a dark staircase — we've only just begun.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at the world the novel inhabits — the Thames, the markets, the institutions — and what it truly cost to be poor in Dickens's London.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — which is to say, with rigour, pleasure, and a good deal of argument.
I'm your host, and today's segment turns on one of the novel's great dramatic engines: Bella Wilfer's moral reckoning — and the elaborate, some might say reckless, mechanism by which she is tested.
To take that apart with me, I have three remarkable guides.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moralist of the old school, and a reader who insists that what a novel is finally about is the individual soul under pressure.
Professor James Blackstone — legal and social historian, who will remind us what the world of this novel actually cost, in real institutional and human terms.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living — who hears in this prose what the rest of us merely read.
Let's begin at the foundation: the dead patriarch, old John Harmon, and what his will tells us about virtue and money in this novel.
One of the things that strikes me most forcibly about this novel is how Dickens plants, at its very root, a paradox about wealth and moral incorruptibility.
Old John Harmon — the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail, as Dickens calls him — despised humanity, mistrusted everyone, and yet was compelled to acknowledge that some people simply could not be bought.
Dickens gives us the psychology of it with great precision.
He tells us that the old miser had perceived —
"the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
The wealth is powerless — not the miser, mark you, but the wealth itself.
Dickens is telling us, at the outset, that integrity is not a commodity — and that a man who has made money his god can nonetheless, in extremis, recognise that fact.
Edmund is right to start there, because that dead man's will is the engine that drives everything that follows.
And from a legal standpoint, what is remarkable is the sheer power the testator retains from beyond the grave.

The Boffins are named as trustees; Bella is effectively conscripted as a potential heiress on terms she never agreed to; and John Harmon Junior is made to inherit a fortune tied to a marriage he had no hand in arranging.
That is the lived reality of Victorian testamentary law — the dead hand reaching forward through time, shaping the choices of the living.
And Dickens understands the cruelty of it perfectly well, even as he also, as Edmund says, grants the old man a kind of grudging moral lucidity.
'The dead Jailer of Harmony Jail' — I mean, you can't improve on that as an epithet.
It's almost heraldic — as if the old man had a coat of arms with a lock and a money-bag on it.
But what James is pointing to is something that colours every scene involving Bella: she has been willed — not loved, not wooed — willed, like a piece of furniture.
And Bella knows it, which is precisely what makes her so prickly and so sympathetic in the early sections of the book.
And yet John Harmon Junior doesn't simply present himself and claim his inheritance.
He devises a scheme — one that stretches credibility, some would say, to its absolute limits — to observe Bella before she can know who he is.
Oliver, as a performer, how do you read that confession scene where Harmon lays out the whole plot?
It's a bravura piece of narration — and Dickens does something very cunning with it.
He gives us the scheme in Harmon's own voice, retrospective and slightly bewildered, as if Harmon himself can hardly believe he went through with it.
Harmon describes how he and Radfoot agreed to dress as common sailors, and throw themselves into Bella's neighbourhood.
"The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way."
'Trying to put ourselves in her way' — as if Bella Wilfer were a destination one simply stumbles upon.
It's simultaneously touching and absurd, and I think Dickens wants us to feel both.
I want to resist the temptation to call it merely absurd, though.
Because Harmon himself, in that same extended confession, tells us precisely what he was afraid of.
He feared, he says —
"the dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil."
That is not the reasoning of a schemer or a romantic fool — that is moral timidity confronting a genuine ethical dilemma.
He uses the phrase 'moral timidity' himself, which is a phrase of quite remarkable honesty for a man under these circumstances.
The dilemma is real, I grant that — but there is something we should not elide, which is the extraordinary power differential at work here.
Harmon chooses to test Bella — but Bella has no idea she is being tested.
He gets to observe, to judge, to withhold himself — while she is simply living her life under financial and social pressures that he could, at any moment, relieve.
And this brings me to a passage I find genuinely harrowing in this context — Lizzie Hexam's account of the child she tends.
Lizzie says of this child, whose father is, like his own father, a weak, wretched, trembling creature —
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
'If she ever had one' — that parenthetical is the most quietly devastating thing in this part of the novel.
Bella's test is being conducted at the level of minor social embarrassment; this child's existence is the actual human cost of the world the novel inhabits.
That juxtaposition is entirely intentional on Dickens's part — and James has put his finger on why it works.

He keeps showing us the outer radius of poverty and degradation precisely so that Bella's dilemma — which is, after all, a dilemma about whether to be mercenary when rich people are offering you money — doesn't become the whole moral universe of the book.
But I'd also say — speaking as someone who has read Mr Boffin's scenes aloud a great many times — that Dickens gives the comedy an equally sharp edge in passages like the charity patrons speech.
Mr Boffin, confronted with a mountain of charity circulars, erupts with this magnificent catalogue —

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The repetition is pure comic music — and it's also a perfectly aimed satirical dart at the vanity of philanthropic respectability.
Mr Boffin's instincts are sound, even when — or perhaps especially when — he is performing the miser.
He sees through the apparatus of charitable self-congratulation with the directness of a man entirely uncorrupted by social ambition.
'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?' — you couldn't put it more precisely if you had a month to compose the sentence.
And yet the novel's resolution is not satirical — it is, in the end, rather tender.
That scene in the counting-house — Rokesmith rushing in, catching Bella in his arms — is Dickens at his most nakedly sentimental.
And the passage earns it, I think, because of how carefully the whole moral architecture has been laid.
Dickens writes —
"My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!"
"And not only that even — but Bella, after hanging her head for a moment, lifted it up and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place!"
'Her head's chosen and lasting resting-place' — that is not sentimental confectionery.
That is the language of moral settlement — a soul that has found its proper home.
I won't quarrel with the beauty of the writing — it is beautiful.
But I'd note that the resolution also requires Bella to have been tested — and to have passed — before she is rewarded with full knowledge of who she has actually married.
The novel's emotional logic grants Rokesmith the right to have conducted his experiment — and then grants him the girl as its prize.
That is a moral structure worth examining, even if the scene itself moves us.
James is right to name it — and I think the exclamation marks in that passage are doing some of the work here.

Dickens punctuates the scene with this breathless, almost incredulous energy — 'which one might have thought astonishment enough for one dose' — as if he himself can barely believe Bella has got there.
And I think that's Dickens earning his own happy ending — by making it feel miraculous rather than inevitable.
The test was, as James says, morally complicated — but the moment of recognition is, on the page, and in the voice, genuinely joyful.
A joyful resolution made possible by a morally complicated journey — which is, in miniature, the shape of a great deal of this novel.
From the dead miser's will to the counting-house declaration of love, we've traced the arc of Bella Wilfer's reckoning — and found it to be something rather richer than a simple redemption story.
My thanks to Sir Edmund, Professor Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan for a discussion that has been, I think, exactly as rigorous and as pleasurable as the novel deserves.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been talking about Dickens's extraordinary range — the way this novel can move from the sublime to the grotesque and back within a single chapter.
This segment, we want to sit with what I'd call the comedy of discomfort — those moments where the novel makes us laugh and then immediately makes us feel slightly guilty for laughing.
Edmund, I want to start with you, because there's a moment near the very beginning of the novel that I think encapsulates this perfectly.
Yes — and it is one of those passages that announces, quite definitively, what kind of novel this is going to be.
Gaffer Hexam has just dredged a body from the Thames — a dead man's pockets have been relieved of their contents.
And then Dickens does something that is almost outrageously comic, given the circumstances.
The passage reads:
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
That triple rhythm — chinked, blew, spat — is a kind of black comedian's trick.
The money has come from a drowned man, and Gaffer is performing a folk superstition over it as casually as a market-day farmer.
That word 'hoarsely' is the masterstroke, isn't it.
He doesn't say it briskly or cheerfully or even guiltily — he says it hoarsely, as if the ritual itself is worn smooth with use.
This is not the first time Gaffer has done this.
As a performer, I find that rhythm almost irresistible to read aloud — once, and once, and once — it has the quality of a charm, a hex.
And then it just — stops.
What strikes me is the complete ordinariness of it for Gaffer.
The riverside trade in bodies was a recognised, if thoroughly disreputable, occupation in mid-Victorian London.
What the law made of the property found on drowned men was genuinely murky — there were real arguments about who had the right to those pockets.
So the 'luck' Gaffer is invoking isn't merely superstition — it is also something like a professional courtesy to whatever forces govern this particularly grim trade.
And then, considerably later in the novel, Riderhood turns this whole world on its head with his accusation of Gaffer.
There is a passage where Riderhood, who is about as trustworthy a witness as one might imagine, makes his formal declaration.
He says:
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
Now, the comedy here — if comedy is the right word — is that the accusation is delivered with all the gravity of a magistrate's pronouncement by a man who is manifestly crooked.
Dickens understands that the forms of justice can be performed by the unjust — and that this is both comic and terrifying.
That repetition — 'his hand and no other' — is Riderhood performing certainty he doesn't have.
On stage, in the dock, in the pulpit — it is the rhetoric of absolute conviction, and Dickens gives it to an absolute scoundrel.
Which brings me to a passage I was assigned that works in almost exactly the same way — the Deputy Lock and poor Betty Higden.
Yes — do take us there.
Betty Higden is fleeing — she's old, she's exhausted, she is terrified of the workhouse — and she encounters this official at the lock.
And he pockets her coins — one by one, mind you, not in a handful but one — by — one — while simultaneously declaring his own virtue.
The passage is almost perfectly constructed for performance:

"I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow; here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry; and I won't stand in your way. Go where you like."
That stage direction buried inside the narration — 'as if this particular portion of his humble gains' — is Dickens doing something quite extraordinary.
He's narrating the man's self-deception while the man is engaged in the act of self-deception.
It is funny. And then you remember who Betty Higden is, and what she's running from. And it isn't funny at all.
That portrait of institutional venality at the lowest level is historically exact.
The lock-keepers, the relieving officers, the workhouse gatekeepers — these were men of negligible income who exercised small but real power over desperate people.
And the ideology they deployed — I am a working man, I ask nothing of no one — was precisely the ideology that justified grinding the faces of people worse off than themselves.
The humor Dickens extracts from it doesn't soften the indictment — it sharpens it.
I'd slightly resist the word indictment, if James will permit me.
Because an indictment implies a prosecutor, and Dickens is something more unsettling than a prosecutor.
He makes us laugh at the Deputy Lock before we despise him — and that implication of our own pleasure is part of the moral work of the novel.
And then — to end on something that feels quite different — Edmund, you have that passage with the train.
Which to my mind is the novel leaving comedy behind entirely.
It is one of the most remarkable passages of descriptive prose in the whole of Dickens.
The train is crossing London, crossing the river — and listen to what Dickens does with it:

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river:
bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
The violence of 'bomb-shell' after the quiet accumulation of that long sentence is — well, it silences me, which is not easily done.
And then Dickens turns on a pin and compares the train's indifference to that of Father Time himself.
Comedy, satire, gothic horror — and then this. The novel contains multitudes.
And yet — to end where we began, with the comedy — I keep coming back to that Mrs Boffin passage I was given.
Because after all the darkness, all the river mud and the drowned bodies and the Deputy Locks of this world, Dickens allows himself something quite unguarded.
Mrs Boffin is explaining why John kept delaying the revelation to Bella — why he could never quite bring himself to end the deception and claim his inheritance.
And his excuse, repeated three times with that same incantatory rhythm we heard in Gaffer's passage, is this:
"She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer."
It is funny, and warm, and — if you've read four hundred pages to get here — rather moving.
The comedy of discomfort has, by the end, become a comedy of earned happiness.
That is a beautiful place to leave this segment — Gaffer's hoarse superstition over a dead man's coins, and John Harmon's tender unwillingness to stop being poor.
The same rhythm, entirely opposite hearts.
Coming up: we'll be turning to the novel's women — and asking what this book, for all its generosity, dares and does not dare to imagine for them.
Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Charles Dickens's last completed novel and opens it up, chapter by chapter, idea by idea.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the world of dust — the great mounds of refuse that underpin the Boffin fortune, and the very particular moral atmosphere that fortune generates.
With me today are three guests whose different lenses on this novel make for, I think, genuinely illuminating conversation.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished close readers of the Victorian novel alive — a man who believes that what great fiction does, above all, is test individual character.
Professor James Blackstone brings legal and social history — he knows what the real institutions behind Dickens's satire actually looked like, and what it truly meant to be destitute in the 1860s.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has brought more classic novels to life on audio than perhaps anyone — approaches every page as a performer first, listening for the rhythm and the timing.
We begin with the Boffins and the flood of letters that descends on them the moment Nicodemus Boffin's inheritance becomes public knowledge.
Dickens turns the charitable letter-writing industry of Victorian England into one of the most corrosive comic passages in the whole novel.
The passage absolutely crackles — it's a setpiece, a complete comic performance in miniature, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing with the rhythm of it.

He gives you this ascending absurdist list first — fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, twenty-seven organs — the numbers themselves are the joke, each one more preposterously specific than the last.
And then he slows right down for the kill — the ducal letter.
He describes it like this:
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six words of physical description — and the Duke is already ridiculous.
The fatness of the envelope does the moral work — you feel the self-importance before a word of the letter is read.
What strikes me is the postscript — Dickens calls it 'thoughtful,' which is of course perfectly withering.
The Duke of Linseed's letter has been lithographed by the hundred, yet it presumes intimacy — 'My Dear Sir,' addressed to a man the Duke has plainly never met.
What Dickens is anatomising here is not merely hypocrisy — it is the complete severance of form from substance.
The language of warmth and fellow-feeling has been industrialised — printed in bulk, signed with a stamp, stripped of any human content whatsoever.
Burke wrote of the necessity of what he called the 'little platoons' — the local and human bonds of genuine society.
This is the opposite: the simulacrum of benevolence manufactured at scale and at profit.

The institutional charity sector in the 1860s was genuinely enormous and genuinely corrupt — there were hundreds of societies of this precise type, maintained largely to provide income for their secretaries and prestige for their patrons.
Dickens's description of charities as 'mostly in difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print and paper' is not satirical exaggeration — it is fairly close reporting.
Parliamentary select committees in that decade repeatedly found that charitable organisations spent more on administration and publicity than on relief.
What Dickens adds — and this is the specifically literary insight — is the class mechanism by which the wealthy are made to feel personally responsible for every institutional deficiency in England.
It is Boffin's notoriety, as Dickens puts it, that marks him — and notoriety in this context simply means having money and being known to have it.
And then we move from the corporate beggars to the individual ones — and this is where it gets genuinely extraordinary.
There's a line about the 'documents' these individual petitioners enclose that I find almost too good to read aloud without pausing to collect myself.
Dickens says:
'they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf'
The butchery of that simile — the total contempt compressed into it — is just magnificent.
It's also very funny, which is important — because what follows is genuinely quite dark.
The catalogue that follows is structured as a kind of taxonomy — daughters of generals, devout wives, inspired beggars, nobly independent beggars — each category a distinct moral type.
What unites them — and this is the moral centre of the passage — is self-deception dressed as dignity.
Consider the nobly independent beggars — those who 'in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross.'
Their pride in not wanting money is the very instrument by which they demand it — a beautiful inversion.
One cannot read this without thinking of what Johnson called 'the last refuge of a scoundrel' — though in this case patriotism has been replaced by moral self-regard.

There is one category in that list that moves me beyond the satirical register entirely, and that is the beggars of punctual business-habits — those who threaten to be 'cold in death' at a quarter to one on Tuesday if no money arrives.

Dickens gives them comic specificity — the quarter to one, the memorandum of heartless circumstances — but behind it is the very real phenomenon of suicide threats in begging letters, which the Metropolitan Police documented extensively.
The humour and the horror are inseparable — and that is precisely where Dickens is most truthful.
Desperation, when it has to perform itself in writing to a stranger, frequently does take on a quality of absurd theatre.
Let's move from those who pursue the Boffin fortune from outside to the Boffins themselves — settled into their grand mansion, which Dickens describes with characteristic precision.
The image Dickens reaches for to describe the house tells us almost everything about what wealth means in this novel.
The cheese.
Dickens compares the mansion to — and this wants reading exactly as he wrote it:
'an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites'
You could spend a happy afternoon unpacking that single sentence.
The aristocracy as a mouldy cheese — too old, too large, breeding things that feed on it.
And Boffin — good, decent, bewildered Boffin — as someone who has somehow come to own this cheese without the faintest idea what to do with it.
The metaphor is crueller than it first appears.

An aristocratic family cheese is a cheese that has been aged, that derives its value from time and tradition — and Dickens is saying, with absolute composure, that the aristocracy is something organic that has gone off.
What I find particularly fine is Boffin's response — he regards the parasites as 'a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty.'
He accommodates his condition with a kind of sturdy philosophical acceptance that is, in its way, more dignified than anything the cheese's supposed aristocratic owners ever managed.
The term 'Legacy Duty' is doing specific legal work there — it was a real inheritance tax, graduated by relationship to the deceased, and Boffin has of course come into his fortune via a will.
Which brings us, naturally, to the will — or rather to the other will, the one that Silas Wegg believes he has found and that he reads to Mr Venus with such theatrical self-congratulation.
The terms Wegg describes are genuinely extraordinary — John Harmon gives Boffin the Little Mound only, and leaves everything else to the Crown.
The justification Wegg reads out is worth hearing in full — it tells you exactly what kind of man old John Harmon was:

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
Never made friends, rebellious family — the entire biography of a miser compressed into a subordinate clause.
And 'quite enough for him' — the posthumous meanness of that phrase.
Old Harmon is still managing Boffin from beyond the grave — still deciding what Boffin deserves, still measuring out the portion.
There's a whole gothic story of miserly paternalism in five words.
And Wegg, of course, believes this document gives him power — which brings us to perhaps the most morally serious passage in this cluster.
Dickens on Wegg hovering outside Boffin's house — this is a passage I find genuinely disturbing in its accuracy about human nature.
He writes:

'Power (unless it be the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.'
The parenthesis is everything — 'unless it be the power of intellect or virtue.'
Dickens grants the existence of worthy power, but only in that brief subordinate clause — and then returns immediately to the kind of power that actually flourishes.
What's legally interesting about Wegg's position — and Dickens understood this — is that Wegg's power is entirely contingent on a document whose validity is itself uncertain.
He has power because he believes he has power, and because Boffin does not yet know he has it — it is pure informational asymmetry.

The image of stripping the roof off like a house of cards is striking because a house of cards has no structural integrity — Wegg's power structure is itself as fragile as what he imagines destroying.
And yet Wegg feels it as pleasure — 'a treat which had a charm.'
Dickens gives Wegg the vocabulary of a man enjoying a particularly satisfying pudding after a good dinner — and makes that domesticity of evil deeply unsettling.
Wegg is not a tragic villain — he's a mean-spirited little man who has stumbled into a moment of leverage and cannot help but savour it.
Which is, in some ways, more frightening than tragedy.
And there we have Bella Wilfer — another figure whose relationship to the Boffin fortune is more complicated than it first appears.
In one brief internal monologue, Dickens gives us Bella's whole attitude to money, class, and the man who will eventually become her husband.
It's a marvellous little passage — Bella thinking rather than speaking, which means Dickens can let her be thoroughly, honestly disagreeable without quite endorsing it.
She reflects:
'to have Pa's lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off!'
'Pa's lodger' — that's the full depth of Rokesmith's status in Bella's imagination at this point.
She doesn't yet see him — she sees his social category, and finds it impertinent.
What I think is important to hold onto — and I say this against what I suspect will be James's instinct to condemn Bella immediately — is that her snobbery is self-aware.
She knows she is mercenary — she is almost proud of it, as a kind of honesty that others lack.
Dickens is not creating a villain here — he is creating a character whose moral education the novel will conduct before our eyes.
I wouldn't condemn Bella — I'd contextualise her.
A young woman in 1864 whose only asset is her attractiveness and whose social position depends entirely on the man she marries — her calculation is not vanity alone, it is rational self-preservation.

What Dickens makes visible, through Bella's irritation, is how completely the marriage market colonises a young woman's interior life — even her resentments are framed in the language of eligible suitors.
Dust, parasites, begging letters, posthumous misers, and a young woman calculating her prospects in her father's borrowed house — this is Dickens at his most panoramic.

What emerges from all of these passages, I think, is a remarkably consistent moral vision: that money, once accumulated, generates its own ecosystem of deception — institutional, individual, and finally internal.
In our next segment, we turn to the other side of that equation — the people at the very bottom, for whom survival itself requires a kind of performance.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the great mystery at the novel's heart — the question of who John Harmon really is, and what he's doing.
In this segment we go deep into the revelation — the Dutch bottle, the disguise, the final reckoning with Silas Wegg.
Edmund Leigh brings his eye for moral character — what does it cost a man to live under a false name?
James Blackstone reminds us what was actually at stake legally when a will was buried in a rubbish heap.
And Oliver Trevelyan — who has spoken these scenes aloud more than anyone — brings the performer's instinct for where the drama lives in the prose.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because before we get to Harmon himself, we have to understand why the Boffins matter so much to this whole architecture.
The Boffins are the moral centre of the novel, and I think people sometimes forget that because they're so wonderfully odd.
But the passage where Boffin describes standing up for young John Harmon against his brutal father — that's where you feel the whole thing underneath.
And Dickens gives Boffin this extraordinary piece of physical detail to carry the weight of it.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
And then the kicker — "received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
Three words. Three words that do the work of a paragraph.
That's Dickens writing for the voice — the repetition, the full stop, the weight of it landing exactly where it should.
What strikes me about that passage is precisely what Trevelyan has identified — but I'd put it slightly differently.
Boffin isn't recounting a social grievance. He's bearing witness to a particular act of domestic tyranny, and he's doing it with love.
The black straw bonnet spinning across the yard — that bonnet tells us everything about Mrs Boffin's practical, unsentimental goodness.
She wore it "as a matter of convenience" — not vanity, not fashion. Convenience. She is a woman who gets on with things.
And when old Harmon sends it spinning, the gesture is contemptible precisely because it is so petty — the cruelty of a small man.
This is what Dickens does supremely well — he locates the moral dimension of a life in the physical particularity of an object.
And of course those scenes of Boffin and Mrs Boffin defending the boy establish the moral claim that justifies everything that follows.
Because the question the novel is really asking isn't just who gets the money — it's who deserves it.
Which brings me to the Dutch bottle — the buried will — because that is where the legal and the moral become fascinatingly entangled.
Boffin finds a later will — one that excludes Harmon and his sister entirely — and he buries it in the Mound rather than destroying it.
Harmon explains it to Wegg with extraordinary precision.
"That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father."
"That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister — then already dead of a broken heart — by name."
"Dead of a broken heart, by name" — that is an accusation in a subordinate clause, which is a very specific kind of savagery.
Now, Boffin's instinct to bury the document rather than destroy it is legally astute — destruction of a testamentary document was potentially criminal.
He was afraid, the text tells us, to destroy it "lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive, might be an offence at law."
There's something almost comic about a man of Boffin's instinctive goodness suddenly having to think like a lawyer.
But the scene I find irresistible is the confrontation with Wegg — because that's where Harmon finally gets to let rip.
And Dickens is almost gleeful about it — "suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will."
Then the line that follows — and it's a line I've always loved performing —
"and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out."
The formal diction — "for leave" — against the naked physical threat. That's the whole joke and the whole point.
Harmon is still the gentleman even while he's banging Wegg's head against the wall.
That tension is in fact the crux of Harmon as a character, is it not.
He has spent the bulk of the novel suppressing himself — his name, his identity, his legitimate claims — in order to test and be worthy of the life he wants.
So when he finally acts — when he seizes Wegg by the cravat with what the text calls a "sailor-like turn" — there is a genuine release of pent-up moral energy.
And yet — and this is what interests me most — even then, Harmon is operating with a plan.
He tells Wegg he has two more "short speeches" to make — because he hopes they will torment him.
The revenge is deliberately crafted, not improvised. This is a man of considerable self-command, even in fury.
Blackstone nods — that's exactly right. The surveillance of Wegg is meticulous.
Harmon tells him — and this is a key detail — that they waited until the last possible moment deliberately.
He says as much directly, and it's worth hearing in the novel's own words.
"I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
Sloppy — this great, lumbering, good-natured creature — as a secret agent.
The comedy is real, but so is the point: Harmon's world has been watching Wegg, gathering everything needed for maximum impact.
The deception is answered by a counter-deception, longer and more patient and more complete.
There's a beautiful symmetry in that — Wegg, who has been playing a long game of false loyalty and concealed discovery, is himself out-played at every step.
And that paper he's clutching — the will from the Dutch bottle — Harmon tells him it's now "worth less than the rotten cork."
The rotten cork. In three volumes of scheming, that's where it ends.
I always pause a beat there when I'm recording it. Let the listener feel the deflation.
What this segment opens up, I think, is how carefully Dickens has been building the moral architecture all along — the Boffins' loyalty, the buried will, Harmon's patient self-concealment.
Every element clicks into place precisely because it was always there, waiting.
In our next segment, we turn to what Harmon's disguise costs the people who love him — and what the novel asks us to make of that sacrifice.

segments.title: Dickens at the Mirror: Technique and Truth

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.

I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the great technical achievements of the book: the way Dickens uses mirrors, doorways, and moments of self-confrontation to trace Bella Wilfer's moral development.
With me today are three guides I couldn't do without.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been reading novels as moral explorations of individual character — and who will not let us mistake a literary device for a political manifesto.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who keeps us honest about what Dickens's world actually looked like — the institutions, the poverty, the stakes.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more classic novels aloud than anyone alive — brings us the text as performance, as rhythm, as something written to be heard.
Let's begin with a question of technique: what does Dickens actually do, moment by moment, to show us a character changing from within?
What strikes me first, and most forcibly, is the economy of it.
Dickens doesn't lecture us about Bella's contradictions — he places her in front of a looking-glass and lets her interrogate herself.
The passage I keep returning to is her soliloquy in her own room after Mr Boffin has spoken rather too frankly about money.
She thinks: 'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself.'
And then — and this is the crux — she asks herself, with genuine severity: 'Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
The looking-glass is not decoration — it is the mechanism of conscience.
She cannot lie to her own reflection, even when she cannot quite tell herself the truth in any other way.
Edmund is absolutely right about the looking-glass, and I'd add that it's one of the most performable moments in the entire novel.
There's a comic relish in the phrasing — 'you inconsistent little Beast' — that tells you Dickens is enjoying himself enormously.
But it's funny because it's painfully accurate — and that's the tightrope Dickens walks throughout Bella's arc.
Then look at what he does with exactly the same technique just a few chapters later, when Bella is listening to Lizzie Hexam.
Bella has been holding forth about money and advancement — and Lizzie's selfless love lands on her like a blow.
Dickens gives us: 'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
And she literally gives herself a poke in the side — a penitential poke, he calls it.
The comedy is the conviction — you can't fake that kind of self-reproach.
I want to hold the comedy at arm's length for a moment, because the social stakes here are rather serious.
Mr Boffin's advice to Bella about money isn't aberrant — it is the perfectly rational counsel of a society in which a woman without fortune had no security whatsoever.
So when Bella disparages him for expressing exactly what she believes, and then attacks herself for the inconsistency, the comedy has a dark underside.
She's not simply vain — she's trapped in a set of values the whole culture has handed her, and she's beginning, just beginning, to feel their weight.
And then compare that against what Lizzie Hexam says — Lizzie, a woman with far fewer options than Bella could imagine.
Lizzie tells Bella: 'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
That sentence — 'anything my life can give me' — is devastating in context, because what Lizzie's life can give her is very little.
And Dickens places it directly in Bella's path, as a kind of mirror of a different sort — not vanity, but values.
James puts it precisely — and it bears on something I think is easily missed when we focus on the comedy of Bella's self-scolding.
Lizzie's confession to Bella is not merely a plot mechanism — it is an act of trust extended to someone who, at this point, has not fully earned it.
And Dickens captures the surprise of it beautifully — Lizzie says: 'I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.'
The grammar itself enacts the surprise — 'a moment before you came in; but you came in.' Short, plain clauses. The rhythm of a mind turning.
This is precisely what I mean by moral imagination as technique — the form and the meaning are indivisible.
You know what's extraordinary — and Edmund has led us straight to it — is that the same novel holds two completely different registers of self-examination.
Bella examining herself in the looking-glass with comic ferocity — and then this other image, which is quieter and I think more haunting.
Rokesmith standing in a doorway — watching Bella, as Betty Higden walks away.

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
'Away from paralysis and pauperism.' Read that aloud and tell me Dickens doesn't know exactly what he's doing with sound.
The alliteration is almost brutal — and it has to be, because Betty Higden's courage in the face of those twin terrors is exactly that.
But Rokesmith is still watching Bella — standing alone — and the double gaze, his on her and ours on him, compresses so much feeling into so little space.
That image of Betty Higden trudging through the streets — away from the workhouse system she so dreads — is doing more than poetic work.
The Poor Law of 1834 had made indoor relief — the workhouse — the primary mechanism of public assistance. Betty Higden's terror is entirely rational.
'Paralysis and pauperism' — Dickens pairs them as if they were equivalent fates, and in that world, they very nearly were.
The bodily decay and the institutional humiliation — both strip you of self-determination. Both are, in their way, a kind of death.
What makes the passage technically remarkable is that Dickens refuses to sentimentalize it — the old figure has 'steady bright eyes,' and she is simply trudging. Determined, not tragic.
Edmund, Oliver, James — what you've traced across these passages is something Dickens does with extraordinary consistency: he finds the technique that matches the moral weight.
The looking-glass for vanity confronted. The doorway for love observed. The trudging figure for courage without applause.
In our next segment, we'll ask how that technique holds up across the novel's larger structure — and whether all the mirrors finally point in the same direction.
We've spent this episode tracing the great currents of Our Mutual Friend — the river, the dust, the dead weight of money.
But I want to close by asking what the novel ultimately makes of transformation — of people changed, revealed, or unmasked by wealth.
Sir Edmund, let's begin with Bella Wilfer — and what Dickens is doing when he shows us Mr Boffin's corruption through her eyes.
The genius of these chapters is that Dickens gives us the moral catastrophe entirely through Bella's perception.
She does not moralise. She simply looks — and what she sees is devastating.
Dickens writes that she ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her eyelashes.
And she saw — and I think this phrase is one of the most compressed moral portraits in the novel —
"a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face."
Three nouns. Three sins, if you like. And the word 'once' doing extraordinary quiet work.
That openness is not merely lost — it is retrospectively mourned. The man he was makes the man he has become worse.
And it doesn't stay in the register of private moral decline for long, does it.
Because Boffin turns almost immediately to the explicitly transactional — to giving Bella her instructions for how to live.
He tells her, in the most unctuous possible tone — and Dickens uses that word, unctuous, which is perfectly chosen —
"Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich."
Now, that phrase — 'live and die rich' — is presented as the summit of human ambition.
It is also, historically, precisely the language of self-made Victorian prosperity — the rhetoric of the self-help manuals, the penny press.
Dickens is not caricaturing something marginal. He is holding up a mirror to the dominant ideology of his moment.
I wouldn't quarrel with dominant ideology — though I'd frame it somewhat differently.
What Dickens shows us is not a system corrupting a man — it is a man surrendering to a temptation that was always latent.
That is the older moral tradition — and it is, I think, the more disturbing reading.
The cloud was always there. It only needed the money to reveal it.
Both of those readings are true simultaneously — which is why performing Boffin is such a gift and such a problem.
Because you have to play his warmth as real — the Golden Dustman who genuinely loved this girl — and then you have to darken that memory retroactively.
And then — and this is where Dickens is simply playing a different game from anyone else — you get Sloppy.
The great unmasking. Dickens waits until the very last moment and then pulls the curtain back with an almost theatrical violence.
Listen to how it reads — this is the moment Wegg, that magnificent small villain, finally gets his comeuppance:
"Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete."
"Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's."
'A face that was Sloppy's.' Four words. The most delicious sentence ending in the book.
Dickens could have written 'it was Sloppy.' Instead he gives you that face — specific, personal, triumphant.
What strikes me about that passage is its structural echo of the whole novel's argument.
Everything in this book is in disguise. The dust mounds conceal wealth. John Harmon conceals his identity. Boffin conceals his goodness.
And Sloppy conceals a whole head beneath a bandage. The comedy is doing serious work.
In a world where wealth corrupts perception, the only honest currency left is the surprise reveal — the moment when the surface finally gives way to what was always underneath.
I find I cannot improve upon that as a summary of the novel's method.
The surface gives way. And the face that is revealed — whether it is Sloppy's wholeness or Bella's essential goodness — is always the truer thing.
Dickens is, in the end, an artist of revelation — not of despair.
Money as corruptor, disguise as survival, the face beneath the bandage — Our Mutual Friend keeps its secrets and then gives them back with interest.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — three readers who have made this novel come alive today in ways I'll be thinking about for a long time.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. Until next time.

Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.
c9:p30.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt

      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s

      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing

c61:p86.text:
Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.

c63:p42.text:
‘And so, my good and pretty,’ pursued Mrs Boffin, ‘you was married, and
      there was we hid up in the church-organ by this husband of yours; for he
      wouldn’t let us out with it then, as was first meant. “No,” he says,
      “she’s so unselfish and contented, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then, when baby was expected, he says, “She is
      such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then when baby was born, he says, “She is so
      much better than she ever was, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I must
      wait a little longer.” And so he goes on and on, till I says outright,
      “Now, John, if you don’t fix a time for setting her up in her own house
      and home, and letting us walk out of it, I’ll turn Informer.” Then he says
      he’ll only wait to triumph beyond what we ever thought possible, and to
      show her to us better than even we ever supposed; and he says, “She shall
      see me under suspicion of having murdered myself, and  you  shall see how
      trusting and how true she’ll be.” Well! Noddy and me agreed to that, and
      he was right, and here you are, and the horses is in, and the story is
      done, and God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all!’
c63:p42.summary: Mrs Boffin completes the narrative: John repeatedly postponed revealing himself because Bella kept improving; only after much urging does he agree to test her by allowing her to witness suspicion of his involvement in his own murder.
c63:p42.best_quote: She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.
c25:p0.best_quote: like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
c40:p97.summary: Wegg cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house, fantasizing about his power to destroy it, demonstrating how power appeals to base natures.
c40:p97.best_quote: Power (unless it be the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.

c25:p17.text:
‘A little too much, I think,’ Miss Bella reflected scornfully, ‘to have
      Pa’s lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off! A little
      too much, indeed, to have the opportunities opened to me by Mr and Mrs
      Boffin, appropriated by a mere Secretary and Pa’s lodger!’
c25:p17.summary: Bella internally rails against Rokesmith's presumption in claiming her attention and excluding eligible suitors.
c25:p17.best_quote: to have Pa's lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off!

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.
c8:p39.best_quote: I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c64:p97.text:
‘That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills
      made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything
      absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and
      reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
      That Dutch bottle was found by my noble benefactor and yours, after he
      entered on possession of the estate. That Dutch bottle distressed him
      beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast
      a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable
      youth, to deserve. That Dutch bottle, therefore, he buried in the Mound
      belonging to him, and there it lay while you, you thankless wretch, were
      prodding and poking—often very near it, I dare say. His intention
      was, that it should never see the light; but he was afraid to destroy it,
      lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive,
      might be an offence at law. After the discovery was made here who I was,
      Mr Boffin, still restless on the subject, told me, upon certain conditions
      impossible for such a hound as you to appreciate, the secret of that Dutch
      bottle. I urged upon him the necessity of its being dug up, and the paper
      being legally produced and established. The first thing you saw him do,
      and the second thing has been done without your knowledge. Consequently,
      the paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you—and I should like
      to shake the life out of you—is worth less than the rotten cork of
      the Dutch bottle, do you understand?’
c64:p97.summary: Harmon explains how the Dutch bottle was found by Boffin after entering the estate, buried in the Mound to hide its contents, and later exhumed without Wegg's knowledge.
c64:p97.best_quote: That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.

c64:p95.text:
‘I mean to knock your head against the wall,’ returned John Harmon,
      suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will; ‘and I’d
      give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out. Listen, you
      scoundrel, and look at that Dutch bottle.’
c64:p95.summary: Harmon violently interrogates Wegg while ordering Sloppy to hold up the Dutch bottle, explaining its significance and his own indebtedness to Boffin.
c64:p95.best_quote: and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.

c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p99.summary: Harmon explains that they discovered Wegg's find through Venus, watched him closely, and deliberately prolonged his deception to maximize his disappointment.
c64:p99.best_quote: I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c42:p156.text:
The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential
      poke in the side.
c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’
c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.
c42:p162.best_quote: I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.

c31:p125.text:
The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled,
      and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the
      determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the
      streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.

c38:p42.text:
Bella ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her
      eyelashes, and she saw a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and
      conceit, overshadowing the once open face.
c38:p42.summary: Bella observes a dark expression of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit shadowing Mr Boffin's formerly open countenance.
c38:p42.best_quote: A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’

c38:p47.best_quote: Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.

c64:p67.text:
Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head,
      Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with
      fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete. Who, untying his tied-up broken
      head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy’s.
